content: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arthropod-borne virus belonging to the genus Alphavirus, transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes, primarily Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. The disease caused by CHIKV is characterized by an acute febrile phase lasting two to five days, followed by a prolonged period of joint pain, particularly in the extremities. In some cases, this joint pain can persist for years. Prevention primarily involves mosquito control and avoiding bites from infected mosquitoes. Currently, there is no specific antiviral treatment for chikungunya, but symptomatic relief can be achieved through medications. The term chikungunya originates from the Makonde language, meaning that which bends up, referring to the stooped posture caused by the arthritic symptoms of the disease. The virus was first identified in 1952 during an outbreak on the Makonde Plateau, located between Tanganyika (now Tanzania) and Mozambique. Chikungunya is closely related to the O'nyong'nyong virus. CHIKV is a member of the Togaviridae family and the Semliki Forest Virus complex, sharing similarities with Ross River Virus, O'nyong'nyong virus, and Semliki Forest Virus. Both innate and adaptive immune responses play a role in the pathogenesis of CHIKV infection. In vitro studies show that human epithelial cells, endothelial cells, primary fibroblasts, and monocyte-derived macrophages are permissive to CHIKV, with viral replication being highly cytopathic but susceptible to type I and II interferons. In vivo, the virus replicates in fibroblasts, skeletal muscle progenitor cells, and myofibers. In the United States, CHIKV is classified as a Category C priority pathogen, requiring Biosafety Level 3 precautions for laboratory work. Chikungunya must be differentiated from other diseases presenting with flu-like symptoms, such as fever, headache, fatigue, joint pain (arthralgia), and muscle pain (myalgia). Differential diagnoses include dengue, influenza, measles, rubella, malaria, and yellow fever. The virus was first described in Tanzania, Africa, in 1952. Since then, outbreaks have occurred in Africa, Asia, Europe, and regions surrounding the Indian and Pacific Oceans. In late 2013, the first local transmission of CHIKV in the Americas was reported in Caribbean countries and territories. Local transmission indicates that mosquitoes in the area have been infected with the virus and are spreading it to humans. Individuals traveling to regions where the virus is endemic, such as the Caribbean, Africa, Asia, and islands in the Indian Ocean and Western Pacific, are at risk of infection. Those at higher risk for severe disease include newborns infected around the time of birth, older adults (≥65 years), and individuals with pre-existing medical conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease. Complications from chikungunya are rare but can include uveitis, retinitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, nephritis, bullous skin lesions, hemorrhage, meningoencephalitis, myelitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and cranial nerve palsies. Most patients recover without significant issues, but some may experience persistent joint pain (arthralgia) for months or even years. Chikungunya infection can present as either asymptomatic or symptomatic following the bite of an infected mosquito. The most common symptoms in symptomatic cases include fever, joint pain (arthralgia) or polyarthritis, and a maculopapular rash. Physical examination often reveals fever, skin rashes, and joint swelling with effusions. There are no pathognomonic laboratory findings for CHIKV infection. However, laboratory abnormalities may include mild thrombocytopenia (platelet count >100,000/mm³), neutropenia, lymphopenia, and elevated liver function tests. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are typically elevated. There is no specific antiviral therapy for chikungunya virus. Treatment focuses on symptom management and maintaining proper hydration. Paracetamol is the preferred medication and should be administered in all suspected cases without waiting for serological or viral confirmation. Suspected cases should be kept under mosquito nets during the febrile period to prevent further transmission. In the absence of an effective vaccine, the only available method to prevent chikungunya virus infection is by reducing human-vector contact. This includes measures such as using insect repellents, wearing protective clothing, and eliminating mosquito breeding sites.
